meta.note: Generic straight one-handed sword — representative of the medieval European arming sword.
Real weapon: Japanese katana, the curved single-edged sword of the samurai class, prized for its differential-hardened edge.
Generic battle axe — representative of the one-handed Viking/Frankish battle axe.
Generic combat dagger/knife, used historically as a sidearm and close-quarters backup weapon.
Generic thrusting spear — the most common infantry weapon across most of pre-gunpowder history for its reach and low cost.
Real weapon: Roman gladius (gladius Hispaniensis) — short, double-edged sword built for tight-formation stabbing rather than wide swings; core weapon of the legions from ~200 BC.
Real weapon: Ottoman kilij — a curved, single-edged cavalry sabre with a distinctive flared 'yelman' tip, used from the 15th century onward for powerful draw-cuts from horseback.
Real weapon: Arabian saif — a curved single-edged sword widespread across the Arabian Peninsula and North Africa, used for slashing cuts in mounted and foot combat alike.
Bonus addition. Real weapon: Viking-age double-edged straight sword (e.g. Ulfberht-type blades), a costly status weapon reserved for wealthier warriors of 8th-11th century Scandinavia.
Bonus addition. Real weapon: Chinese dao — a broad single-edged sabre, one of the '18 arms' of traditional Chinese martial arts, used by infantry and cavalry for centuries.
Real weapon: Greek xiphos, a short leaf-bladed sidearm carried by hoplites as a backup to the dory spear, used for close-in stabbing once formations broke down.
Real weapon: Greek dory, the primary hoplite spear (~2.5m) that formed the backbone of phalanx warfare — reach and formation discipline mattered more than the weapon's individual power.

Real weapon: Mongol composite recurve bow — laminated horn, wood, and sinew gave it far more power for its size than a European longbow, and it could be fired accurately from horseback at a full gallop, the technological backbone of the Mongol Empire's conquests.
Real weapon: Persian shamshir, a strongly curved single-edged sabre optimized for slashing draw-cuts from horseback — its design later influenced the Ottoman kilij and Indian talwar.

Real weapon: French AN XI light cavalry sabre — a curved slashing blade suited to the charge-and-cut tactics of Napoleonic light cavalry, distinct from the straight thrusting swords of heavy cuirassier regiments.

Real weapon: iklwa, the short stabbing spear credited to King Shaka Zulu, who is said to have redesigned Zulu warfare around close-quarters stabbing rather than throwing spears at range — central to Zulu victories such as Isandlwana in 1879.

Real weapon: the rapier, a long thin thrusting sword that dominated European civilian dueling from the 16th-17th centuries — built for precision point-work rather than the cutting power of earlier arming swords.

Real weapon: the Scottish claymore, a large two-handed great sword ('claidheamh-mor') used by Highland warriors — its size traded some accuracy for the heaviest cutting power of any blade in this dataset.
Real weapon: the tomahawk, a light hand axe used across many Native American nations for both close combat and throwing, later widely adopted and traded by European colonists as well.
